notes: How each source's protocol names reach a definition. A name not listed here is looked up among the IRP definitions (protocols.json) by its own name. 'native' names are read into the shipped protocol definitions (library/protocols) by public_ir_sources.py; 'irp' defines a source's own variant in place (with its 'name'); 'set' gives parameter values as IRP expressions - over D, S and F for IRDB, over A (the address) and C (the command) as little-endian numbers for Flipper; 'refused' says why a name cannot be used. tests/test_ir_source_coverage.py checks every name the sources use is here or defined.

kaseikyo.name: Kaseikyo (Flipper)
kaseikyo.why: Flipper's address is the vendor (M, N) in its middle bytes, genre 1 (D) and genre 2 in its low byte and a 2-bit id on top; its command is 10 bits, the low nibble beside genre 2 and the rest under the id. Defined here rather than as IrpTransmogrifier's Kaseikyo: the last byte is the XOR of the three before it, as Flipper sends it, which that definition's checksum matches only when the vendor's parity nibble is 0 (checked against IRDB's Panasonic 128,0: Power 61)
